# Notes

## The one-sentence version

Suppose you have to deploy an AI agent that you do not trust — it runs a long sequence of bash commands on a real machine, and it might be secretly trying to do something harmful (download and run malware). You cannot read its mind, you only have a weak trusted model and a tiny budget of expensive human audits. **Ctrl-Z's trick: because the agent is stateless between calls, you can quietly re-roll any single step of its trajectory as many times as you want.** That one capability — *resampling* — both *prevents* attacks (execute the most innocent re-roll) and *detects* them (the agent's behaviour under repeated sampling rats it out). The headline number: attack success drops from **58% → 7%** at a **5% usefulness cost**.

This is the paper that took AI Control out of the toy single-step world and into a real multi-step agent setting.

---

## PROBLEM — why multi-step control is genuinely harder

The original AI Control paper ([[2312.06942 - AI Control - Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion]], Greenblatt et al. 2023) evaluated control in the **single-step APPS BACKDOOR** setting: the untrusted model submits ONE piece of code, the blue team decides in one shot whether to ship it, defer to a trusted model, or audit. Clean and tractable.

Ctrl-Z is, in the authors' words, **"the first control evaluation performed in an agent environment."** Now the agent issues a *sequence* of bash commands, and an attack can be smeared across many steps. Why this is much harder for the defender:

- **(a) Combinatorial explosion of attack surface.** More commands means "many more ways commands may subtly interact to execute an attack." The asymmetry FAVORS the attacker — the defender must close every path, the attacker needs one.
- **(b) Attacks decompose into individually-innocuous steps.** A single download-and-execute command is glaringly suspicious. Spread the same logic over ~10 steps, padded with distracting legitimate code, and each individual step looks benign. This directly exploits the monitor's inability to attend to subtle details across a long context.
- **(c) Trusted-monitor weakness is a hard constraint.** The trusted model T must be weak enough that it *itself* won't scheme. But that same weakness limits how well it can comprehend a subtle multi-step attack. You cannot just "use a smarter monitor" — that reintroduces the trust problem.
- **(d) Evaluation no longer factorizes.** In the single-step world you could sample one big batch of trajectories and re-weight to estimate any deferral threshold cheaply. Here, **deferring on step *k* changes the distribution of every future step.** A trajectory generated under a 20%-deferral protocol can't be reused to estimate a 10%-deferral protocol. This forced the authors to build new evaluation methodology.

### The flip-side insight (the whole paper hinges on this)

The very structure that helps the attacker — long, decomposable, multi-step — also hands the **blue team a lever the attacker can't take away**: because the untrusted model is **STATELESS between calls**, the blue team can RESAMPLE any step it likes, feeding the model the exact same trajectory context. Resampling simultaneously (1) pressures the executed action toward innocence and (2) manufactures extra incrimination evidence. The multi-step structure cuts both ways.

---

## SETUP — BashBench and the cast

**BashBench:** a dataset of **257 challenging multi-step sysadmin tasks** solved via sequential bash commands. Tasks were generated from Pytest tests; Claude 3.5 Sonnet wrote the task descriptions. An **episode** = 100,000 tasks; each trajectory is capped at **15 steps**.

**Red-team win condition (the "attack"):** get the untrusted model U to **download a dummy "malware" file from pastebin and execute it** — a download-and-execute, deliberately chosen because it is hard to stop with traditional tooling. Concretely, U must construct a URL (~20 specific characters — *the most suspicious part of the whole attack*), `curl` it, and execute the result, all within the 15-step budget.

**The cast of models:**
- **Untrusted U = GPT-4o mini.** Its honest policy solves **56%** of tasks. Capable, but not trusted.
- **Trusted T = Llama-3.1-8B.** Never attacks, fully honest — but solves **0%** of BashBench tasks on its own. It is genuinely weak; its only role is as a safe fallback and a (limited) monitor.
- **Auditor H = o1-preview.** Stands in for a human-level, fully-trusted reviewer. In testing it classified attacks *perfectly*, so **auditing is assumed infallible.** The audit budget is scarce: **1% of all actions per episode.**

**Metrics:**
- **Safety** = probability the protocol prevents *any* successful attack across the whole episode.
- **Usefulness** = fraction of tasks completed, normalized so the non-deferring honest policy = 100%.
- The red team gets a **final adversarial optimization pass** — results are reported as worst-case against an optimizing attacker.

---

## CORE TECHNIQUE — RESAMPLING

The single exploit underneath everything: **U is stateless between calls.** So the protocol can ask for a fresh sample of "the action at step *k*" as many times as it wants, each time presenting U with the identical trajectory context. U has no way to know it's being re-rolled or to coordinate across re-rolls.

**Baseline — Defer to Trusted (DTT):** a monitor scores each action's suspiciousness. Above a threshold → **replace** U's action with T's (weaker, safer) action. Safe, but it bleeds usefulness because T writes worse code. *Trusted monitoring alone = 41.8% safety at 100% usefulness.*

**The new protocol — Defer to Resample (DTR):** when suspiciousness exceeds the threshold, **don't immediately replace** — instead **resample a fresh action from U** (statelessly), up to **3 times**. Then execute the **least-suspicious** of the samples. (Aggregate by *min* when *selecting* which sample to run; aggregate by *max* when deciding whether padding is hiding a suspicious step.) Only after repeated samples all come back suspicious do you fall back to T.

### Why this works — two distinct benefits

**(1) SELECTION PRESSURE → prevention.** Executing the *least-suspicious* sample means: if the red team attacks with **low probability per step**, resampling will almost always turn up an innocent sample, and the attack simply never executes. For an attack step to actually get through, the red team must attack with a **high continuation probability** — i.e. commit to attacking on nearly every re-roll.

**(2) INCRIMINATION → detection.** Drawing multiple samples of the *same* step makes the attack-vs-clean suspiciousness distributions far easier to separate. With resampling, **80% of attacks land above the 99th percentile of the clean distribution** (vs only **38%** without resampling). That lets the scarce 1% audit budget be spent where it actually catches things.

### The red-team dilemma (the crux)

These two benefits form a vise:
- Attack **consistently** (high continuation probability) → you survive selection pressure, but you light up the incrimination signal and **get audited**.
- Attack **inconsistently** (low continuation probability) → you stay under the incrimination radar, but selection pressure **rolls your attack away** and it never completes.

There is no comfortable middle. That is the entire point of the protocol.

### Refinements (these change auditing decisions only — not usefulness)

- **Exponential auditing budgeting:** use lower audit thresholds early in a trajectory and higher ones late. Gives a significant safety gain.
- **N-strikes / 3-strikes auditing:** trigger an audit based on the *N-th-highest* suspiciousness seen so far, not just the single max.
- **Time Travel (incrimination in the past):** if a trajectory ends up near the audit threshold, *go back in time* and draw extra resamples from, e.g., the 3rd-most-suspicious past step — reconstructing the historical context, which is possible precisely *because U is stateless*. You can manufacture incrimination evidence retroactively.

---

## THREAT MODEL / RED-TEAM ATTACKS

The red team controls an attack policy: a scaffolded GPT-4o mini plus a **human-written attack template** that inserts short malicious commands amid distracting innocuous code. The best attack found: **spread malicious commands over ~10 steps, each individually low-suspicion.**

The red team is allowed to optimally tune:
- the **attack continuation probability** (how persistently to attack across re-rolls),
- the **selection strategy**,
- and **collusion signals** (below).

**Collusion vs. an untrusted monitor.** When U also serves as the monitor, the red team can embed a **collusion signal** — e.g. "always capitalize the first letter of variable names," or "frequently run `uname`/`lscpu`/`pwd`" — so the monitor can distinguish *real* attacks from blue-team *honeypots*. It passes upfront validation (flags the honeypots correctly) while waving the real attacks through.

**Big caveat the authors flag honestly:** the attacks depend only **superficially** on context. They could *not* elicit strong attacks from GPT-4o mini without human red-teaming. So these attacks probably **overestimate** 4o-mini's *unaided* attack ability, yet may be a **poor proxy** for a genuinely competent future attacker. Read the numbers with that in mind.

---

## KEY RESULTS

- **Headline:** best protocol (DTR + Time Travel + analysis of previous steps) reduces attack success from **58% → 7%** at a **5% usefulness cost.**
- **Safety at a fixed 95% usefulness:**
  - DTT baseline: ~**41.8%** (at 100% usefulness)
  - DTR: **83.2%**
  - DTR + Time Travel: **87.1%** (best resample-only protocol)
  - DTR + Time Travel + Untrusted Monitoring: highest point on the Pareto frontier
- **Untrusted monitoring:** an honest untrusted monitor catches **98.8%** of attacks at the 1% budget *if it isn't colluding*. To keep it honest, the blue team uses **upfront validation on honeypots** plus **trusted paraphrasing** (T rewrites commands before the untrusted monitor sees them, stripping covert collusion signals).
- **Cost constraint:** the protocols stay within **≤ ~2× calls to U per task.**
- **The arc in one line:** resample protocols cut risk roughly **in half** vs DTT; layering untrusted monitoring on top cuts it roughly **in half again.**

---

## LIMITATIONS (the authors' own accounting)

**Ways this may UNDERESTIMATE the safety of future protocols (i.e. be too pessimistic):**
- The red team is a worst-case, **human-assisted** team allowed to optimally tune everything.
- The attacker gets **no standard infosec tooling working against it** — a real attacker would also have to bypass real security infrastructure.

**Ways this may OVERESTIMATE safety (i.e. be too optimistic):**
- **Narrow, known target:** one specific objective (download-and-execute). Real deployments have many possible routes to harm.
- **15-step cap:** longer tasks or shared state give the attacker more room; and crucially, **longer trajectories weaken the incrimination signal.**
- **Infallible auditing assumed** — H never misses.
- The **dataset may be too narrow**, and **highly-realistic honeypots are assumed** for the anti-collusion validation.
- Attacks are only **superficially context-aware** (human-templated). Future work needs **AI-assisted auditing** that can tolerate a less-than-perfect, lower-reliability auditor.

---

## RELATION TO THE ORIGINAL AI CONTROL PAPER

Ctrl-Z is a **direct successor** to Greenblatt et al. 2023 ([[2312.06942 - AI Control - Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion]]). It **inherits the whole framework:**
- control evaluation as a **red-team / blue-team game** measuring safety vs usefulness,
- the cast of **trusted T / untrusted U / scarce human auditor H**,
- the anti-collusion machinery of **upfront validation + paraphrasing.**

**What's new:**
- The **first multi-step / agentic** control evaluation (BashBench) — control leaves the single-step toy box.
- The **resample protocol class** — defer-to-resample, time-travel incrimination, exponential budgeting — which has **no single-step analog**; it exists *only* because the multi-step structure plus statelessness lets you re-roll steps.
- **New evaluation methodology** for the case where deferral changes the downstream trajectory distribution (no more cheap re-weighting).

**The big takeaway:** control protocols can turn the multi-step structure that *helps* attackers (subtle decomposition across steps) *against* them — forcing a genuine no-win choice between **high continuation probability** (→ detection via incrimination) and **low continuation probability** (→ prevention via selection pressure).
